chapter: Sidney Bechet and the Paris festival
title: Charlie Parker afraid to follow Bechet at the Salle Pleyel
summary: Parker, nervous about following Bechet, was encouraged by Moore; the crowd booed a German band off.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Charlie Parker was there along with Al Haig.

Kenny Dorham and James Moody and who else was there -- the drummer, Max Roach. Anyway I had finished my set with Hot Lips Page and Don Byas and there's a bar down the basement under the Salle Pleyel where the Festival was and I'm down there and I'm listening to Sidney Bechet hold that audience spellbound and all the noise that come in there and I'm down there having a beer and I'm talking with Charlie Parker, Charlie was almost in tears when he says to me, 'I can't follow that ole man. Listen to the people upstairs. Man he should close the show. I shouldn't close the show, he's the main man here. I mean, he's been here before and he should close the show, I don't want to go up there.' I said, 'Now, Charlie, you have your own thing, you play your thing. That's what you're contracted to do.' He said, 'Yeh, I know, Chief, but I don't like to do it'and I might say this at this point, that at this Festival there was two factions. The way French concerts are conducted, there are two factions there, they're trying to outdo each other. On the progressive side, the

faction of Charles Delaunay was in evidence there by the appearance of Charlie Parker and the modernists, and the emergence of Hugues Panassie, who is with the traditional guys like Sidney Bechet and they pit them all together, you know. I think it's mostly a money-making proposition to draw the people in. But it was Sidney Bechet that held that whole crowd in there and I'm going back downstairs when Charlie said, "I hate to follow that old man, that old man's got the people by the -- what am I going to do?" I said, "Charlie, you do your thing," that's what I said to him.

So at one point I heard the band from Germany come in to follow Bechet and they booed them off. They made so much noise that they couldn't play. Bechet was off the bandstand and this band from Germany came on stage and started to play and these people, the whole multitude of them, the people that were there, jam-packed in the Salle Pleyel, made so much noise, they don't want it, they want Bechet. They made so much noise that the band stopped playing and poor guys, they got off the bandstand. And when Bechet came back on for an encore, the whole place is in a bedlam. When Bechet started to play again, the

crowd got quiet to listen. And this is what Charlie was telling me, you know. "I can't follow that old man." I said, "No, Charlie, do your own thing." "I love the way you blow, now you get yourself straight and go out and blow."

So finally Bechet was finished and they're waiting for Charlie Parker. So he said, "Okay, Chief, here I go. I don't know what's going to happen but I'm going to blow like you said." "Go ahead, Charlie. Just think of our old days in the Kentucky Tavern in Kansas City. Remember those days, Charlie?" He said, "Yeah, Chief. Okay." He went upstairs. He played, Charlie played and he sounded great, although the place emptied quite a bit when Bechet left. Charlie got nice applause, sort of courtesy applause. But to this day I believe Sidney Bechet won that whole crowd in. He was the star. He was the one behind all that conglomeration of the Festival of Jazz. 1949.
